facts.text: A model is a simplified mathematical or computer-code description of a real thing that behaves closely enough like the real thing to answer a particular question; model fidelity describes how closely it does so.
facts.quote: A model is a simplified description of a real thing, written in mathematics or computer code, that behaves like the real thing closely enough to answer one particular question, and its fidelity is how closely it does so.

facts.text: A braking model uses machine speed, mass, slope and ground surface to predict the distance the machine travels before stopping.
facts.quote: A braking model takes the machine's speed, mass, the slope and the ground surface and gives back how far the machine travels before it stops.

facts.text: A sensor model uses a virtual scene to predict what a camera, radar or lidar would have measured.
facts.quote: A sensor model takes a virtual scene and gives back what a camera, radar or lidar would have measured.

facts.text: A terrain model describes the shape and softness of the ground.
facts.quote: A terrain model describes the shape and softness of the ground.

facts.text: Model parameters are numbers set once, such as haul-truck mass or the rate at which brakes build up pressure.
facts.quote: The parameters are numbers set once, such as the mass of a haul truck or how fast its brakes build up pressure.

facts.text: Higher model fidelity requires more measurements to build the model, more computing time to run it and more expertise to check it.
facts.quote: Higher fidelity costs more: more measurements to build it, more computer time to run it, more expertise to check it.

facts.text: A simple ground model assigns a friction number to a surface, whereas a high-fidelity ground model simulates sand or clay grain by grain.
facts.quote: A simple ground model is a friction number painted onto a surface. A high-fidelity one simulates sand or clay grain by grain

facts.text: The booklet reports a grain-by-grain ground model running 50 to 200 times slower than real time.
facts.quote: the booklet reports such a model running 50 to 200 times slower than real time [Chapter 11].

facts.text: The booklet describes four sensor-model families, ranging from a few lines of noise added to perfect detection to full simulation of the physics of light or radio waves.
facts.quote: For sensors, the booklet describes four families, from a few lines of noise added to a perfect detection up to the full physics of light or radio waves [Chapter 6].

facts.text: Model fidelity is specific to the test question rather than a single rating for an entire simulator: a simulator valid for worker-detection perception tests may still incorrectly predict machine sliding distance on wet gravel.
facts.quote: A simulator that predicts well whether a worker is detected may be valid for perception tests and still wrong about how far the machine slides on wet gravel [Chapter 5].

facts.text: The booklet recommends layered models for each machine family: a fast threshold model for very large parameter sweeps, a stability model to derive deceleration limits and a high-fidelity multibody model only for selected cases that could disprove the simpler models.
facts.quote: a fast threshold model for very large parameter sweeps, a stability model to derive deceleration limits, and a high-fidelity multibody model only for the selected cases that could prove the simpler models wrong [Chapter 8].

facts.text: The virtual-validation plan relies on models standing in for a prototype that does not yet exist.
facts.quote: The whole virtual-validation plan rests on models standing in for a prototype that does not yet exist.

facts.text: A model with less fidelity than a test demands can give false confidence even after millions of virtual runs.
facts.quote: If a model is less faithful than the test demands, millions of virtual runs give false confidence

facts.text: Using more model fidelity than needed risks spending the four-month virtual-validation window on computing instead of evidence.
facts.quote: if it is more faithful than needed, the four-month window is spent on computing instead of on evidence [Chapters 1, 8, 11].
